notes.h: Meaning of equality of opportunity (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Equality of opportunity means every student has a fair chance to access, take part in and benefit from education, whatever their background.
points: Equal access means every student can enrol and attend; equal outcomes means students finish with similar results, which does not follow automatically from equal access.
Students begin school from different starting points, so equal treatment alone may not give equal opportunity.
Equity means giving extra support in proportion to need, so that students at a disadvantage can reach the same level of achievement.
Barriers to equality of opportunity include gender, socio-economic status, disability, family background and location.

notes.h: Gender and equality of opportunity (Higher Level only)
points: Boys are more likely than girls to leave school early and to have lower literacy levels at second level.
Subject choice can be gendered: fewer girls than boys take subjects such as Physics, and fewer boys take subjects such as Home Economics.
Teacher and parent expectations can differ by gender, which can influence the subjects and courses students consider.
Schools can widen opportunity by encouraging students to choose subjects on the basis of ability and interest rather than gender stereotypes.

notes.h: Socio-economic status and equality of opportunity (Higher Level only)
points: Families with low incomes may struggle to pay for books, equipment, uniforms and school activities.
Allowances, book rental schemes and grants reduce these costs, but they do not remove the wider gap in resources between families.
Parents with higher levels of education are more likely to have high expectations for their children and to be able to help with schoolwork.
Students from lower socio-economic groups are more likely to leave school early and less likely to progress to third level.
Students in lower-status groups may be placed in lower streams or sets, which can limit the grades and courses open to them.
Teacher expectations and the locality of a school can reinforce the effects of socio-economic status.
Disadvantaged students include those from low-income families, Travellers, Roma, students from migrant families, students with disabilities, homeless young people and young people in care.
Students from migrant families may need language support in English or Irish, and their qualifications from other countries may not be recognised.
The DEIS (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) programme identifies schools serving disadvantaged communities and gives them extra staffing and supports.
Students living in disadvantaged areas may face poor housing, poor health, lack of study space and limited access to after-school activities.
An early school leaver is a young person who leaves school before completing a senior cycle programme such as the Leaving Certificate.
Early school leaving is more likely among students with poor attendance, low literacy and numeracy, or learning difficulties.
Bullying, family problems, poverty, and negative peer pressure all increase the risk of leaving school early.
Leaving school early limits access to further and third-level education and to skilled employment.
Early school leaving is linked with unemployment, low pay, poor health and social exclusion later in life.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that every student has a fair chance to access, take part in and benefit from education, regardless of background.
Providing extra support in proportion to need so that students who start at a disadvantage can reach a comparable level of achievement.
A family's social and economic position, usually based on income, occupation and education level.
A young person who leaves school before completing a senior cycle programme such as the Leaving Certificate.
The situation where a student's background, location or circumstances limit their access to education and their achievement in it.
Grouping students by ability for particular subjects or for the whole school year, which can affect the grades and courses open to them.
Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools, the Department of Education programme that gives extra supports to schools serving disadvantaged communities.
Patterns in which students choose subjects differently by gender, often reflecting stereotypes rather than ability.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which socio-economic status can limit equality of opportunity in education.
questions.model: Any two, three marks each: families with low incomes struggle to pay for books, equipment and uniforms and so may be excluded from full participation; parents with lower levels of education may have lower expectations and less ability to help with schoolwork; students from lower socio-economic groups are more likely to leave school early and less likely to progress to third level; placement in lower streams can limit grades and courses.

questions.prompt: Analyse how gender, socio-economic status and early school leaving affect equality of opportunity in education, referring to one initiative that responds to disadvantage.
questions.model: Gender: boys more likely to leave school early and to have lower literacy; subject choice shaped by gender stereotypes, with fewer girls in Physics and fewer boys in Home Economics. Socio-economic status: cost of books, equipment and uniforms; allowances, book rental and grants reduce but do not remove barriers; parental education and expectations; lower socio-economic groups less likely to progress to third level; streaming and teacher expectations. Early school leaving: definition as leaving before completing senior cycle; risk factors such as poor attendance, low literacy, bullying, family problems and poverty; consequences such as limited access to further and third-level education and skilled work, and later unemployment and social exclusion. Initiative: DEIS, which gives extra staffing and supports to schools in disadvantaged communities, with an explanation of how it addresses one of the barriers named.
